genZNote: Turns wine and cider into vinegar by oxidizing ethanol straight into acetic acid — one of the oldest 'biotechnology' processes humans have used, long before anyone knew bacteria were involved.

morphology.motility: Motile via peritrichous flagella (some strains) or non-motile
morphology.notes: Highly tolerant of acidic conditions, an adaptation to the acetic acid it produces.

habitat.naturalHabitat: Flowers, fruit, and fermenting plant material
habitat.environmentalOccurrence: Naturally present on fruit surfaces and in unpasteurized wine/cider, where it can spoil the product by continuing fermentation to vinegar
habitat.reservoir: Fruit surfaces, fermenting beverages, industrial vinegar production tanks

culture.media: Glucose-yeast extract-calcium carbonate agar (clear zones form around colonies from acid production)
culture.growthCharacteristics: Obligate aerobe; requires vigorous aeration industrially
culture.colonyMorphology: Small, smooth, often forms a clearing zone in calcium carbonate media from acid production

biochemicalTests.test: Oxidation of ethanol to acetic acid

identificationClues: Obligate aerobe that oxidizes ethanol directly to acetic acid — the biochemical basis of vinegar production and the reason open, aerated wine/cider spoils into vinegar
Highly acid-tolerant, allowing it to keep functioning even as the medium becomes increasingly acidic from its own metabolic byproduct
Clears calcium carbonate agar around colonies due to acid production, a classic diagnostic culture technique
Purely beneficial/industrial in the food production context; not a human pathogen

examFacts.importantTest: Clearing zone on calcium carbonate agar from acid production
examFacts.distinguishingFeature: The classic vinegar bacterium, converting ethanol directly into acetic acid via obligate aerobic oxidation

sources.name: NCBI Bookshelf — overview of acetic acid bacteria and industrial fermentation
